entries.title: Blake Plateau: the largest known deep-sea coral reef
paragraphs: In January 2024, NOAA Ocean Exploration and a coalition of partners (Ocean Exploration Trust, the University of New Hampshire, the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, Temple University and the U.S. Geological Survey) announced the results of a multi-year mapping campaign: a nearly continuous province of cold-water coral mounds on the Blake Plateau, off the south-eastern United States, that is the largest known deep-sea coral reef habitat on Earth.

Published as Sowers et al. 2024 in the journal Geomatics, the study synthesised 31 multibeam sonar surveys and 23 submersible dives gathered over more than a decade. The full coral province stretches up to about 500 km long and 110 km wide, with a especially dense core area -- nicknamed 'Million Mounds' -- some 254 km long and 42 km wide. Across the whole province, automated mapping identified 83,908 individual mound-like peak features, covering roughly 6.4 million acres, an area larger than the state of Vermont.

The reef sits beneath the Gulf Stream, which sweeps warm water and a steady supply of food particles across the plateau at depths of roughly 500-1,000 m -- exactly the conditions the reef-building coral here needs, since it lives far below where sunlight reaches and depends entirely on filtering food from the current rather than photosynthesis.

What you see here: the seabed is real bathymetry from the GMRT Synthesis, showing genuine relief consistent with the mapped mound field, though at this tile's resolution (roughly 53 x 61 m per cell) individual coral colonies and the smallest mounds are not resolved.

entries.title: A dense coral mound cluster
paragraphs: This stretch of seabed shows real, mapped terrain relief consistent with the dense mound clusters described across the wider Blake Plateau province -- roughly 72 m of local relief around this point, with depths in the low 700s to high 700s of metres nearby.

Individual coral mounds in the province vary hugely in scale: most are modest, tens of metres across, but the tallest known mounds rise as much as 90 m (about 300 ft) off the surrounding seafloor. This tile's resolution cannot distinguish individual mounds at the smallest end of that range, but the broad relief you can scan here is genuine survey terrain.

Only the specific claim that any single bump here is a named, individually-mapped mound (rather than general provincial relief) is an inference, not a direct match to a published mound catalogue entry.

entries.title: Desmophyllum pertusum, reef-builder of the deep
paragraphs: The coral that builds these mounds is Desmophyllum pertusum, until recently known as Lophelia pertusa -- a stony, cold-water coral that thrives in total darkness at depths of roughly 200-1,000 m and water temperatures around 4 degrees C. Unlike shallow tropical corals, it has no symbiotic algae and gets no energy from sunlight; instead its polyps filter zooplankton and organic particles carried past by the current. Healthy Desmophyllum pertusum is naturally white; that colour is not a sign of bleaching.

Over thousands of years, generation after generation of coral skeleton accumulates into the mounds you see across this province -- among the slowest-built, longest-lived structures in the ocean, and correspondingly fragile: a single mound can represent millennia of growth that a moment's careless contact could damage.

facts.label: Energy source
facts.value: filter-feeding on drifting particles, no sunlight

entries.title: One mound among thousands
paragraphs: A few hundred metres from the main cluster, this second mound illustrates how the Blake Plateau's coral mounds are not isolated features but part of a near-continuous field -- the mapping behind this province identified 83,908 individual mound-like peaks across the wider area, a first-ever estimate of just how many of these structures exist here.
At about 776 m deep and roughly 400 m from the main cluster, it sits close enough to reach on the same dive, a reminder of just how densely packed this coral province really is.

entries.title: The Gulf Stream overhead
paragraphs: The Blake Plateau sits directly beneath the Gulf Stream, the powerful, warm western-boundary current that carries water (and the food particles deep corals depend on) northward along the US East Coast before crossing the Atlantic. Researchers describe the current as a key reason this reef exists at all: it delivers a steady supply of drifting food to corals that cannot photosynthesise, sustaining growth across a province hundreds of kilometres long.
Currents above and between the mounds carry the drifting food that keeps this dark-water reef alive.

facts.label: Role here
facts.value: delivers food particles and moderates temperature for the reef

sources.title: World's largest deep-sea coral reef found lurking beneath the Gulf Stream — Live Science

entries.title: Between the mounds
paragraphs: Not every part of the Blake Plateau is covered in coral: between mounds, the seabed dips into lower channels and open sediment, visible here as a modest local low point between two mapped mounds.

These lower channels let bottom currents and drifting food particles move between mounds, rather than pooling around any single one -- part of what lets a field this dense keep so many mounds fed at once.
